item.title: Is it normal for the host node to constantly read my SSH info and Fail2ban config?
item.dc:creator: member55
item.description:
English is not my native language, so I translated this with the help of AI.

With so many Linux vulnerabilities surfacing recently and lots of people getting compromised, I started learning more about server security. I learned that the QEMU Guest Agent allows a KVM host to run arbitrary commands on the guest VM. I went ahead and checked the qemu-guest-agent logs across all my machines, and noticed that one of them—hosted on ColoCrossing—behaves differently from the rest.

Roughly every hour, it reads my SSH public key, SSH configurations, and Fail2ban configurations. I don't store private keys on it, so I'm not sure if the read behavior would be different if I did.

My technical knowledge is limited, but this looks suspicious to me. I'm just not sure whether this is actually normal. Has the host node been compromised? Could one of the third-party packages I installed have gotten me compromised? Or is this just routine security scanning and completely normal behavior?

I'm reaching out to the community for help: do any of you see similar activity in your logs?

As a side note, I tried submitting a support ticket several times without success. Logging in and filling out the form went smoothly, but at the very last moment when hitting submit, Cloudflare blocked the request.

Command used:

journalctl -u qemu-guest-agent -e

Log output:

info: guest-file-open called, filepath: /proc/meminfo, mode: r
info: guest-file-open, handle: xxxx
info: guest-file-close called, handle: xxxx
info: guest-file-open called, filepath: /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, mode: r

info: guest-file-open called, filepath: /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/99-admin-ignore.conf, mode: r

item.title: VSYS Host: UA data centers. What happened and where recovery stands?
item.dc:creator: member42
item.description:
Hi everyone,

Many of you have been affected by the outage in Kyiv or have seen it discussed here, so we want to give you a clear picture of what happened and where recovery stands.

What happened

On September 23, the first Russian missile strike hit one of data centers. A few hours later, the second one was hit, and then hit again. Both are now out of operation for an indefinite period.

These were not isolated hits. The strikes also affected other data centers where we have no equipment. This was a wider attack on data center infrastructure.

Condition of the equipment

In the first hours we had no physical access to our hardware and could only rely on information from the data center teams. Once our engineers reached the sites:

  • In data center 1, 100% of our equipment is physically intact.
  • In data center 2, our equipment also survived, but some hardware shows signs of water exposure. These servers need to be inspected before they can be powered on, otherwise recoverable hardware could be damaged.

Virtual services

Rather than waiting for the original facilities to reopen, we moved our virtual infrastructure to another data center selected for its security profile. The majority of affected virtual services are already running there.

Work on the rest continues, and we expect 100% of them to be restored within the nearest few days.

Dedicated servers

This is the harder part. Dedicated servers are the hardware itself, so they have to be physically moved to another facility before they can run again, and we're talking about a very large fleet.

The new facility needs enough space, power, cooling, connectivity and staff to take this volume. It also must not carry an unacceptable risk of a missile strike. We won't move customer infrastructure to the first facility that happens to have space.

We haven't secured such a facility yet, so there is no ETA for dedicated server restoration. We'd rather not give a date we can't stand behind. Once a facility is confirmed, servers will be relocated and restored progressively.

In parallel, we're working on a way for customers to copy their data from dedicated servers before full restoration. We'll contact affected customers directly once a workable process is ready.

Other locations

VSYS Host is fully operational. Support is available, and our locations outside Ukraine are running normally. We're seeing a lot of migration requests, so some dedicated configurations outside Ukraine may soon be temporarily out of stock. If you're planning to move, open a ticket and we'll check what's available.

Full incident report: https://vsys.host/news/two-kyiv-data-centers-hit-within-hours-incident-report-and-recovery-status

We'll keep this thread updated as things progress. Happy to answer general questions here.

Thank you to everyone who has been patient with us.

We've been working through these days without a break to bring everything back, and we'll keep going until every service is restored.

Thank you for your patience, your support, and every kind word we've received. It means a lot to us right now.

item.description:
Hi LET,

My name is Member and I am the founder of ServersCamp.
We are building a cloud provider, https://serverscamp.com

What is it?

We are trying to tune our cloud for databases, and naturally it works great for other workloads too.
To get there we had to do a lot of custom stuff, both in solutions and in architecture.
Also took a lot from the enterprise world.
In theory the whole set should look like this, this is what every VM technically gets:

1. Hardware

We already have 2 types of hardware, old first gen Xeon Scalable and latest EPYC.
No middle ground yet, planning to add Genoa or Milan.

2. Network

No real alternatives here, so Mellanox cards and Mellanox switches, with RDMA, eBGP, PFC.
Software side is OVN.

3. Disks

No local disks at all. What good are they if the node physically goes down.
All storage is SDS, replicated network storage on NVMe disks, default replica 2 for now.
Synthetics showed great results, around 150-160 us qd1.

4. Backups

Here we got inspired by enterprise and went the DR backups way.
Our backup supports multi backend, at the moment the backends are: our S3 (same DC, but outside of SDS), Wasabi and Impossible Cloud.
We also added encryption, possibility to download from the backends and automatic checks that the backup is alive at all.
Meaning, after every backup, besides md5 it also gets physically downloaded and boot is started, we check if the VM was able to start from that backup.

5. Security

We tried, and it seems we succeeded, to integrate Suricata in a way that you can build zero trust even in a flat network.
Beyond firewall rules, we wanted visibility into what's actually happening in the traffic, with the option to block threats inline. For every VM you can enable inline, it stays transparent for everyone, but traffic analysis and interception happens on the underlay network level. Not all functionality works yet.

6. Redundancy and geo

Right now we have one site in Bucharest, Romania, EU.
We don't want to stop at one, so we already made a deal with another provider and are working on the second site. It will give us another location, very good international peering and serious anti-DDoS protection.

=========================================================

Here are our tests:
https://serverscamp.com/docs/benchmarks/block-storage-vs-local-nvme
https://serverscamp.com/docs/benchmarks/hetzner-vs-serverscamp-postgres

Third party:
https://serververify.com/benchmarks/5c644141-aa29-488a-ae48-bd646d3b07b5
https://www.vpsbenchmarks.com/yabs/serverscamp-12c-63gb-20260724-f759f0

=========================================================

It works already.
But our tests are one thing, how the platform behaves under live load is another, and we want to see it.
So we invite anyone interested to come and test our cloud.
We prepared capacity for this on nodes of different generations.

  1. Total slots 50-100. Depends on the load and how much the cluster can take without overall degradation.
  2. Max instance size 2 cores and 4 GB RAM + 100 GB disk.
  3. Please don't use it for abuse, miners and such.
  4. Please don't create multi accounts.

How to start

  1. Register at https://serverscamp.com and confirm your email.
  2. Open a ticket mentioning LET or PM me here. We will set up your account manually and add 25 euro of credit for 1 month.
    Account setup currently needs a card. For LET we do it manually, so you don't need to add one. Until we do the setup, you won't be able to create anything.

We will be adding redeem codes here from time to time and posting updates.
And if you need more, just open a ticket.

Offered $18.30 account credit or a migration to a different location/IP instead. I declined the credit (original payment method only, no account credit).

item.title: Terabit.io || Paid $2,000 for a dedicated server, 52 days later and still nothing
item.dc:creator: member82
item.description:
I wanted to share my experience with Terabit.io because, at this point, I honestly don't know what else to do.

Before placing my order, I specifically asked about the delivery time and was told "it's 2-3 business days on average." I went ahead and paid $2,000 on September 5th for a dedicated server. Today is October 27th. 52 days later, I still haven't received a single server. Not even the temporary replacement they promised me.

Here's a quick summary of what happened:

After the initial 3 days, I started asking for updates. Most of the time, I either got vague answers or no response at all until I followed up again. On September 20th, they finally explained that the CPU they ordered was defective and they were waiting for an RMA from their supplier. I understood the situation and continued waiting.

By October 5th, a full month had passed. I even suggested that they provide me with any available server with lower specs until my original one was ready. On October 6th, they replied that their CPU shipment was delayed due to a supplier backlog and mentioned that they had other CPUs they could offer temporarily if I was okay with a different CPU. I immediately agreed and asked what they had available. Then, once again, silence. Three more days without a response.

On October 9th, after more than a month of waiting and getting nowhere, I finally requested a cancellation and full refund. Their response? Dedicated servers are non-refundable according to their ToS.

Seriously? I paid $2,000 for a server that was supposed to take an average of 2–3 business days to deliver, and more than a month later, they still hadn't delivered anything. How is their supplier's problem supposed to become my responsibility?

They then confirmed they had Xeon Silver servers in stock and eventually offered me one for free as a temporary replacement until my original server was ready. I accepted because, honestly, I just wanted to move forward. But guess what? That server never arrived either.

On October 14th, they told me the setup was almost complete and only some cabling remained. On October 20th, another message saying "The build is almost finished." On October 22nd, after I complained again, they told me the temporary server would be ready that day. The following day, they said they were installing Ubuntu on it.

It's now October 27th, and I still haven't received even the temporary server. Apparently, even installing an OS takes several days.

And that's not even everything. I had to purchase an IPv6 subnet twice for this server. The first one expired without ever being used, and the second has been sitting unused because they still haven't delivered the server. So on top of wasting nearly two months, I've also been losing money.

What frustrates me the most isn't just the delay. It's the complete lack of communication and urgency. I shouldn't have to keep chasing a company for updates on a $2,000 order. They rarely seem to take any initiative to keep me informed.

I understand that hardware issues and supplier delays happen. But 52 days without delivering anything, repeatedly promising a temporary server and failing to provide it, and then refusing a refund because of a non-refundable policy? That's simply unacceptable.

If customers are expected to respect a company's Terms of Service, shouldn't the company also be expected to fulfill its side of the agreement?

I'm not asking for anything unreasonable. I paid for a service I still haven't received, and I believe a full refund is more than justified at this point.

I'm posting this to share my experience and hopefully get some advice from the community.
